# Diagnosing a Dead 1992 GMC Vandura: When Voltage Doesn't Mean Power

You have a 1992 GMC Vandura 2500 with a 5.7L engine, and you are facing a classic "no crank, no start" scenario that has defied standard component replacement. The symptoms have evolved from a "no crank, lights on" state to a total system failure where the dashboard remains completely dark despite the battery reading a healthy 12.8 V. You have already swapped out the starter motor, ignition switch, ignition lock cylinder, and even replaced a burnt 15 A fuse without restoring function.

This progression tells a specific story about where the electrical fault actually lies. The most common misconception in automotive diagnostics is equating battery voltage with system readiness. A reading of 12.8 V confirms the battery has chemical charge and can hold a potential difference, but it does not guarantee that the battery is capable of delivering high-current pulses or that the ground paths are intact. Before replacing any further expensive components like an alternator or ECU, you must verify the integrity of the chassis grounds and the fuel delivery system, as these are the most likely culprits in this specific symptom pattern.

### The Grounding Hypothesis

In older GM vehicles from the early 90s, corrosion or broken wiring at the body ground points is a frequent failure mode. If the main negative battery cable is connected to the post but not properly bonded to the chassis frame, or if the engine block ground strap is compromised, the vehicle will exhibit exactly these symptoms.

When you turn the key, the ignition switch sends voltage to the dashboard and radio. However, for the headlights and interior lights to illuminate, current must return to the negative terminal of the battery through the chassis. If there is a high-resistance connection at the primary ground point (often located near the firewall or under the driver's side floor), you will get zero voltage at accessory points once the load exceeds a certain threshold.

To diagnose this, do not rely solely on a multimeter reading at the battery terminal. You need to perform a voltage drop test across the ground path. Disconnect the negative battery cable and place your multimeter probes: one on the battery post and one on the chassis near the light switch or dashboard lights. If you read more than 0.1 V with the key in the "On" position, you have found your fault. The fix is often as simple as cleaning the ground terminal and ensuring the clamp makes solid metal-to-metal contact, potentially replacing the ground strap if it is frayed.

### Fuel Delivery Considerations

If the grounding checks out, the next logical failure point is fuel delivery. A 1992 Vandura with a 5.7L V8 often uses a mechanical or early electronic fuel injection system (depending on the exact trim and emissions package). If the fuel pump relay has failed internally or if the pump itself has seized, the engine will never turn over because there is no air-fuel mixture to ignite.

You can isolate this by listening for the hum of the fuel pump when you first turn the key to the "On" position (before cranking). You should hear a distinct 2-3 second whirring noise from the rear quarter panel or under the rear seat. If there is silence, but the battery is good, check the main power feed to the fuel pump relay. Often, these relays are located in the under-hood fuse box and can fail open without blowing a fuse initially, especially if they were subjected to heat cycling for several weeks.

### Verdict on Previous Repairs

It is worth noting that replacing the starter, ignition switch, and lock cylinder was the correct direction for the initial "no crank" issue. However, once the system failed completely (lights off), the root cause likely shifted from a mechanical engagement failure to an electrical continuity failure. Continuing to replace components based on the assumption that it is another switch or motor will only increase repair costs without resolving the underlying circuit break.

If you verify solid grounds and still have no power at the dashboard, check the main battery cables for internal corrosion inside the terminals. Sometimes the cable looks fine externally but corrodes internally, creating a high-resistance path that drops voltage under any load other than static measurement. Clean the terminals, tighten all connections, and re-test. Only after exhausting these circuit-level checks should you consider the engine control module or fuel pump as the primary suspect.
